content: 1. Five studies were assessed to have a medium risk of bias (RoB). However, the authors did not provide sufficient information to justify this assessment. 2. The quality of reporting in the systematic review was suboptimal. There was a lack of detailed descriptions of the trials that reported outcomes, no information on relative and absolute numbers, and no forest plots. This made it difficult to confidently assess the certainty of the evidence. 3. The authors reported that one study had a low risk of bias, five had a medium risk of bias, and one had a high risk of bias. 4. The authors did not provide specific details, but based on other outcomes, it is likely that there are serious concerns regarding the evidence. 5. The authors characterized the results across studies as mixed. 6. Five studies compared the intervention to usual care, but the authors did not provide details about the other two studies. 7. The comparisons were made between studies, not within individual studies. 8. Another review (Ruppar, 2017) explored the same question in Black populations. The review found no statistical differences in outcomes when the intervention was delivered by a physician versus not. 9. Another review (Xu, 2018) examined the same question in a Chinese population. Similarly, no statistical differences were observed when the intervention was delivered by a physician versus not. 10. None of the trials included in the systematic review were judged to have a low risk of bias. 11. Based on the narrative description provided by the authors, there appears to be serious inconsistency in the evidence. 12. A systematic review on the effect of interventions to enhance medication adherence included a subgroup analysis. This analysis showed that nurse involvement was not statistically significantly associated with changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP). However, the authors did not provide specific effect sizes, only a p-value for comparisons between nurses, pharmacists, and physicians. 13. Ten randomized trials assessed adherence (no definition provided). Seven of these studies reported improvements in medication adherence following the implementation of a nursing intervention. However, the authors did not provide details about the number of participants. 14. Two systematic reviews (Ruppar, 2017; Xu, 2018) examined differences in the effect of interventions to improve medication adherence when delivered by a physician versus not. Both reviews found no statistical differences in outcomes. 15. Mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, end-stage kidney disease, heart failure, serious adverse events, and patient satisfaction were not reported in the included studies. 16. Although the authors described the trials as being at low risk of bias, the nature of the intervention made it impossible to blind participants, increasing the risk of performance bias. 17. There was statistically significant heterogeneity between subgroups. 18. The authors conducted subgroup analyses to explore the effects of different co-interventions. 19. Differences in the presence and magnitude of effects suggest that self-management interventions may have an effect (or lack thereof) when complemented by other interventions. 20. The certainty of the evidence within each subgroup was moderate, as there were no serious concerns about inconsistency. 21. The number of patients experiencing the event was not reported, making it impossible to calculate this outcome. 22. Most of the studies were judged to have more than one domain at high risk of bias. 23. The authors did not provide sufficient information to assess certain domains of the evidence. 24. A newer version of the systematic review (Sheppard, 2019) was recently published, and its results are consistent with those reported in the earlier review. 25. The authors did not conduct a quality assessment of the included studies in their cost-effectiveness analysis. 26. Team-based care interventions to improve blood pressure control were found to be cost-effective, with 10 studies reporting a cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) of less than $50,000. 27. Underprivileged patients, such as those from lower socioeconomic classes or with limited health literacy, were found to have poorer outcomes in managing non-communicable diseases. 28. Despite evidence of the effectiveness of telemonitoring for hypertension, there is no empirical evidence of its long-term success or generalizability to diverse patient populations. 29. Patients with chronic conditions reported that remote monitoring increased their understanding of their condition, validated their symptoms, and prompted earlier clinical action. 30. Remote monitoring promoted confidence in self-management, including making independent changes to medication regimens. 31. Patients expressed concerns that care provided by non-physicians might become overly focused on clinical data rather than personal interaction, potentially reducing face-to-face consultations. 32. Patients were reluctant to adopt remote monitoring due to concerns about ongoing costs and reduced personal contact with healthcare providers.
